transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-10-15
Start: 15:00 PT
Duration: ~52 minutes
Attendees: Maya (Redwood AE), Daniel (Redwood SE), Sofia (Redwood SE), Aisha (Sparkline Head of ML), Tom (Platform), Priya (PM)

Summary (auto): design session for POC quality eval focusing on golden prompts, regression tests, hallucination detection and scoring.

[00:00] Maya: okay hi everyone, thanks for joining, um we're aiming to sketch out the quality eval plan for the POC today — success criteria, the golden prompt set, and bench / load sizing.
[00:18] Aisha: sounds good, yea we want clear gates for hallucination, like what counts as a failure, and also format fidelity — our EMR templates must be exact.
[00:33] Daniel: right, delta between hallucination (invented facts) and permissible inference is a big one. we'll propose a 3-layer check: semantic correctness, citation/traceability, and format regex checks.
[00:49] Priya: quick context — our main use case is summarization+recommendations for triage nurses, typical prompt length is ~150 tokens, expected model output 40-120 tokens. 95th percentile stdev on output size is kinda tight.
[01:10] Tom: and infra-wise we need VPC-only for PII, so private deployment is likely; but for the POC we can run in hosted with obfuscated data if Redwood's secure env meets SOC2.
[01:28] Maya: noted — we'll send our SOC2 + security one-pager post-call.
[01:34] Sofia: for golden prompts, propose three buckets: canonical summarization prompts, edge-case clinical prompts, and instruction-following/format enforcement prompts. we usually aim for ~30 golden prompts per bucket.
[01:52] Aisha: 30 each sounds fine but can we tighten to 15 must-pass and 15 exploratory? we don't want to blow up labeling.
[02:04] Daniel: yeah 15 must-pass per bucket = 45 must-pass total, plus 45 exploratory — that keeps human review feasible.
[02:16] Priya: how do you measure hallucination? a boolean per output or a graded score?
[02:24] Daniel: good question. we recommend two axes: binary hallucination flag (does the output contain a fabricated clinical fact) and a hallucination score (0-3) for severity. Combine with a format score (0-2) and accuracy/utility (0-5). final pass if hallucination_flag=false AND overall_score >= threshold.
[02:47] Tom: what's threshold number?
[02:50] Daniel: initial rubric: overall_score >= 7 out of 10 and hallucination_flag false. we can tune after initial runs.
[02:59] Aisha: I like numeric thresholds but we need examples. can you, uh, show how an output with a minor hallucination but correct recommendation scores?
[03:11] Daniel: sure. example: model suggests a drug dose not in patient chart — that's severe hallucination -> immediate fail. if it infers likely next step like 'consider ordering CBC' when labs absent — lower severity, maybe score 1 on hallucination but still fail if hallucination_flag is set true by the annotator.
[03:33] Maya: also, format checks: our templates require exact headings: 'Assessment:', 'Plan:' etc. we'll use regex and token-level markers to enforce strict passing.
[03:45] Priya: do you support structured outputs like JSON schemas? we need both human readable plus JSON for downstream ingestion.
[03:52] Sofia: yep we can include schema validation in the pipeline. if JSON parse fails, format_score = 0.
[04:02] Maya: ok let's talk workload sizing for bench. what qps/latency targets do you have, Tom?
[04:11] Tom: production target is 200 rps average, but burstable to 1k for short windows. tail latency 95th pct under 300ms ideally.
[04:22] Daniel: for POC we usually simulate a scaled-down load: a 30-minute load with representative token distribution. we can do a smaller baseline bench at 50 rps and a stress test to 500 rps. would that surface the cost/latency tradeoffs?
[04:38] Tom: yes that should. we also want KV cache performance tested — our workflows reuse patient context a lot.
[04:45] Daniel: good point — we'll include prefix/KV cache scenarios. note: in transcriptions sometimes KV = keev so forgive me if that shows up wrong.
[04:54] Aisha: haha noted. for benchmarks we also need quality regressions tracked across model versions — what's your regression test approach?
[05:03] Sofia: regression harness: run golden prompts + customer sample set each run, collect per-prompt metrics (hallucination_flag, format_score, accuracy_score), and maintain a baseline model snapshot. failures trigger an alert if any must-pass prompt regresses beyond threshold.
[05:22] Priya: do you support automated diffing / visual reports?
[05:26] Daniel: yes, Redwood Console shows per-prompt diffs and we can export CSV w/ per-utterance annotations. we'll also add regression-alert email hooks.
[05:36] Maya: timeline: customer provides 500 de-identified samples, Redwood builds golden prompt set and rubric, run initial bench, then 2-week pilot with weekly regression checks. does that timeline work?
[05:49] Aisha: 2-week pilot is ok, want to include a failover plan if hallucination rates exceed threshold mid-pilot.
[05:56] Daniel: we can set automatic fallback policy — if model variant exceeds hallucination threshold for X minutes we'll route traffic to a safer smaller model or to human-in-loop.
[06:07] Tom: human-in-loop needs latency considerations; we may queue for review for things flagged severe.
[06:12] Maya: noted. let's define success criteria explicitly — what would you consider a green POC?
[06:18] Priya: green = hallucination_rate < 2% on must-pass set, format compliance >= 98%, latency 95th < 350ms on POC infra, and no critical security blockers.
[06:31] Aisha: and acceptable accuracy/utility score >= 4 on average for must-pass prompts.
[06:36] Daniel: we'll codify that and include in the rubric doc.
[06:40] Sofia: labeling logistics: we recommend having Redwood do initial annotation on 200 of the 500 samples to speed iteration, then customer validates another 200, final 100 held out for blind eval.
[06:53] Aisha: sounds fair, but we need to confirm internal compliance process before you annotate.
[06:58] Maya: yes we'll await your sign-off.
[07:02] Priya: training for annotators — will Redwood provide annotation guide?
[07:06] Daniel: yes, a 6-8 page annotation guide with examples, edge cases, and clear hallucination definitions.
[07:14] Tom: on costs — can you produce a ballpark for hosted vs dedicated for the POC?
[07:20] Maya: we'll include an estimated token cost and projected instance hours. Daniel will put together a dedicated vs hosted delta tomorrow.
[07:28] Daniel: one more technical ask — we need the token distribution of your queries (input length histogram, output length histogram) to pick model variants and quantization profiles.
[07:36] Aisha: we'll extract that and send with the sample export.
[07:40] Maya: good. any regulatory or compliance notes?
[07:44] Tom: we need audit logs for model access and inference calls preserved 12 months for audits.
[07:49] Sofia: Redwood Console supports audit logs and we can bump retention for enterprise plan; we'll include that in the security doc.
[07:57] Priya: last thing — hallucination detection tooling: do you use automated external knowledge checkers or human-only?
[08:05] Daniel: hybrid — automated entailment checks and knowledge-base lookups for obvious facts, but humans for edge clinical facts. automated checks catch many but not everything.
[08:16] Aisha: good. ok let's recap next steps.
[08:19] Maya: recap: Maya to send SOC2 + security one-pager and initial golden prompt template; Daniel to send benchmarking config and cost delta; Aisha to provide samples and token histogram; Tom to confirm latency targets formally. schedule bench run for week of 10/27 — agreed?
[08:38] Priya: yes week of 10/27 works.
[08:41] Maya: thanks everyone. we'll follow up in email and share the rubric draft by Tue 10/20. meeting end.

Notes/links mentioned: Redwood POC rubric template (internal link), security one-pager (will be attached), bench config example: redwood.ai/bench-sample (note: placeholder).

Transcript capture notes: occasional mis-transcriptions of acronyms (VPC -> vee-p-c, KV -> keev), conversational overlap, some pauses.
